rows.verified: Respirable crystalline silica can be generated when materials such as concrete, mortar, bricks, sandstone and granite are cut, drilled or ground.
Respirable crystalline silica is fine enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and may be invisible under normal lighting.
Exposure can cause silicosis, lung cancer and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
High-energy tools, dry work methods, enclosed spaces and longer task duration can substantially increase airborne dust.
Work should be designed to reduce cutting and preparation, including using correctly sized or pre-cut materials where practicable.
Water suppression and suitable on-tool extraction are recognised controls for high-dust construction tasks.
FFP3 respiratory protective equipment is generally advisable for high-dust tasks involving silica or wood dust.

The workplace exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica is 0.1 milligrams per cubic metre averaged over 8 hours, and health surveillance is required where there is a reasonable likelihood of silicosis.
Silica controls depend on material composition, tool energy, task duration, enclosure, water suppression, extraction performance, housekeeping and RPE fit.
Silica evidence is material-, task- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level lung-disease probability.
Demolition is construction work and is subject to the Construction Design and Management Regulations 2015.
Clients must appoint designers and contractors with relevant skills, knowledge and experience.
Local-authority building control must normally receive notice at least six weeks before demolition starts.
Clients must provide a competent refurbishment or demolition asbestos survey.
Pre-construction information should cover structural stability, alterations, asbestos and below-ground live services.
The demolition method must be written by a competent person, address the structure and site hazards and specify effective controls.
Planned exclusion, safe-working and debris zones must reflect the demolition technique and the distance debris could travel.
The sequence of work must eliminate uncontrolled collapse and protect workers, neighbouring businesses and members of the public.
Demolition controls depend on structural form, condition, sequence, neighbouring assets, available space, services, asbestos, traffic and public exposure.
Demolition evidence is structure-, project- and site-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collapse or injury probability.
